Two years into my Vabysmo injections, I asked my retina specialist a question I had been carrying for months.

I asked him whether there was anything I could be doing between appointments.

Anything at all. Anything I could take, anything I could change, anything I could eat.

He looked at me across the exam room the way he always does after an injection — kind, tired, on to the next patient — and he told me to eat more spinach.

That was in April 2023. I was 68 years old. I had been getting Vabysmo injections in both eyes every six weeks for two years and one month. I had counted.

I had counted because I keep a spreadsheet.

I want to tell you about the spreadsheet, because it is the reason I ended up writing this letter.

My name is Elizabeth. I am 71 now. I retired eleven years ago from a career as an office administrator at a small architectural firm in Providence, Rhode Island. I spent thirty-two years there. I ran their books, their calendars, their contracts, their permitting paperwork, and their filing systems.

If it needed to be organized, I organized it.

When I was diagnosed with wet AMD in my left eye in March 2021 — three months after cataract surgery, the way it seems to happen for a lot of us — I did the only thing I know how to do when a piece of my life becomes complicated.

I started a spreadsheet.

The spreadsheet has fourteen columns. Date of appointment. Left eye or right eye. Which drug was administered. Dose. Which physician performed the injection. Any side effects during the appointment. Any side effects in the twenty-four hours following. OCT scan findings. Central macular thickness measurement. Visual acuity measurement. Copay amount. Total cost billed to insurance. Mileage to the clinic. Any comments from my retina specialist.

I have three hundred and eighteen rows in that spreadsheet as of last week.

Three hundred and eighteen appointments.

I want to tell you what I found in those three hundred and eighteen rows, because I think you might be where I was two years ago, and I do not want you to spend another two years asking the same question I was asking and getting the answer I was getting.

Here is what my spreadsheet showed.

Between March 2021 and April 2023, my central macular thickness stabilized. My wet AMD stopped its active bleeding. The Vabysmo did exactly what it was designed to do. My retina specialist told me at every appointment that my numbers were where he wanted them to be.

But my visual acuity in my left eye, in the same two-year window, dropped from 20/40 to 20/60.

My central vision was getting worse.

Not from active bleeding. From something else.

Something the injections were not addressing.

I brought this to my retina specialist in April 2023 — the appointment with the spinach recommendation. I brought my spreadsheet. I brought the visual acuity trend line I had graphed at home. I asked him what was happening.

He told me that a decline in visual acuity was normal in AMD patients even when the wet component was well-controlled. He told me the injections were stopping the leak. He told me they were not, and had never been, treatments for the underlying degeneration.

I asked him what was treating the underlying degeneration.

He said we had discussed AREDS2 at my initial diagnosis and I had declined because the zinc bothered my stomach. He said beyond AREDS2, there was nothing else with the same level of evidence. He said to eat more spinach and to come back in six weeks.

I paid my copay. I walked out to my car. I drove home.

I sat at my kitchen table and I did what I have done every time in my life when a person in a position of authority has given me an answer that did not match what I was seeing in front of me.

I did the research.

Not on Facebook. Not on the AMD support groups where everyone tells you what worked for their sister-in-law. On PubMed. On the actual medical literature. The way I used to research zoning ordinances when the architects needed to know what they could build on a specific lot.

I spent six weeks reading.

Here is what I found.

The pivotal anti-VEGF trials — MARINA and ANCHOR, both published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2006 — established the current injection protocol for wet AMD. Those trials were carefully designed. The drug was Lucentis at the time. The protocol was monthly injections. The primary endpoint was preventing vision loss.

The trials succeeded. They showed that anti-VEGF injections significantly reduced the rate of vision loss in wet AMD patients compared to placebo. That is why we have the injection protocol we have now. That is why my Vabysmo appointment happens every six weeks. That is why my central macular thickness is stable.

But if you read the MARINA and ANCHOR papers themselves — not the marketing materials, the actual papers — you will find something the trial authors are explicit about.

The trials were designed to test one specific mechanism. Blocking vascular endothelial growth factor. Preventing the abnormal blood vessels from leaking and bleeding into the retina.

They were not designed to test protection of the photoreceptor cells.

They were not designed to test mitochondrial support.

They were not designed to test antioxidant delivery to the retinal tissue.

The MARINA authors themselves noted, in their discussion section, that a substantial subset of patients in the trial continued to lose visual acuity over the study period even when the neovascular component was well-controlled by the injections.

I recognized myself in that sentence.

Wet AMD has two things happening at the same time.

The first is the abnormal blood vessel growth and the leaking. That is what the injections address. That is why my central macular thickness is stable and my leak is controlled.

The second is the underlying oxidative damage to the photoreceptor cells themselves. That damage has been happening in my retina since before the wet component appeared. It is happening now, between injections. It has been happening in my mother's dry AMD for eight years and she has never had a wet event at all.

The injections were never designed to address the second thing.

Nothing my retina specialist has prescribed me has been addressing the second thing.

Nobody in my three hundred and eighteen appointments ever brought up the second thing until I brought it up myself.

Here is why.

The follow-up research on the underlying oxidative damage in AMD has been accumulating in the medical literature since the late 1990s. Peer-reviewed papers from research groups in the United States, Japan, and Northern Europe have documented that a specific class of antioxidants — carotenoids that cross the blood-retinal barrier and enter the photoreceptor cells themselves — can reach the tissue where the second problem is happening.

The most-studied molecule in that literature is astaxanthin.

Not lutein. Not zeaxanthin. Not the AREDS2 formula.

Astaxanthin.

The clinical trials on astaxanthin and retinal function have been running for more than two decades. They use a specific dose in a specific delivery format. Twelve milligrams per day, delivered in a fat carrier so the molecule can cross into the tissue where the oxidative damage is happening.

That research has never been incorporated into any pharmaceutical protocol for wet or dry AMD.

For a specific reason.

The pharmaceutical companies that make anti-VEGF drugs — Genentech, Regeneron, Roche — have every financial incentive in the world to fund research on molecules they can patent. Ranibizumab was patented. Aflibercept was patented. Faricimab, the drug in my Vabysmo, was patented. Each one generated billions of dollars in revenue.

Astaxanthin is a natural carotenoid produced by a microalgae called Haematococcus pluvialis. It cannot be patented by anyone. There is no company on the planet with a financial reason to spend forty million dollars proving that this molecule addresses the second problem in AMD.

So the research on the injection protocol got funded, and the research on the oxidative photoreceptor damage sat in the medical journals. Both bodies of research are real. Both are peer-reviewed. Only one of them ended up in the exam room where my retina specialist practices.

This is not a conspiracy. Nobody buried anything. The astaxanthin literature is right there in PubMed. Any retina specialist with a library card can read it.

But medicine does not run on library cards. Medicine runs on continuing-education seminars sponsored by pharmaceutical companies, drug-rep visits, and clinical guidelines issued by professional societies whose recommendations are shaped by what the pharmaceutical pipeline has funded. Nobody sends a drug rep to talk to a retina specialist about a natural algae extract. There is no professional society bulletin recommending a supplement that no member can bill through insurance. The pipeline that would carry astaxanthin from the medical literature into my monthly injection appointment simply does not exist, because there is no money moving through it.

That is the finding that made me stop reading and start ordering.

Before I tell you what I ordered, I want to say something plainly.

Nothing I have found in six weeks of reading changes anything about my injection schedule.

I still get Vabysmo every six weeks. I have not missed an appointment since I started. I do not plan to miss one. The injections are addressing the first problem — the vascular one — and that problem does not go away, and it does not stop being urgent, and the day I let it go untreated is the day my wet AMD comes back and takes what is left of my central vision in the left eye.

Astaxanthin does not address vascular leakage. It does not replace anti-VEGF. It is not an alternative to the injections. Nothing in the peer-reviewed literature suggests it does what the injections do.

What astaxanthin does is address the second problem — the oxidative photoreceptor damage — that the injections were never designed to touch.

The injections are the emergency response.

Astaxanthin is the maintenance layer that has been missing from my protocol for three years.

That is why I am taking both.

I want to be careful here, because I have spent enough time reading marketing materials to know that when a supplement claim sounds too good, it usually is.

The reason most astaxanthin products on the market do not produce the results in the clinical literature is that most of them are not the astaxanthin the clinical literature tested.

Three problems, in three bottles out of four on the shelf.

The first is source. Astaxanthin can be manufactured synthetically in a laboratory from petrochemical precursors. It looks similar to the natural molecule. It does not perform the same way in the human body. Synthetic astaxanthin is cheaper and is what fills most private-label bottles. The clinical trials did not use it.

The second is dose. The trials that produced measurable outcomes used twelve milligrams per day. Most retail bottles contain four milligrams. Some contain six. A four-milligram bottle is not a smaller dose of the trial protocol — it is a different intervention entirely.

The third is delivery. Astaxanthin is a fat-soluble molecule. For it to cross into the tissue where the damage is happening, it has to be delivered in a fat carrier. Most retail products are sold as dry powder in a hard capsule. The powder passes through the digestive tract without ever reaching the cells that need it.

If you have tried astaxanthin before and felt nothing, one of those three things was almost certainly the reason.

I spent a week researching brands. I read certificates of analysis. I compared source documentation. I looked at extraction methods, concentration, delivery format, and third-party testing. I applied the same methodology I used at the architectural firm when I was vetting subcontractors.

I chose CoraLume.

Twelve milligrams per softgel — the dose the human clinical trials actually used.

Natural astaxanthin from Haematococcus pluvialis microalgae, ocean-cultivated, not synthesized in a lab. The same source used in the peer-reviewed literature.

Suspended in a fat carrier so the molecule reaches the retinal tissue. Softgel, not dry capsule.

Every batch third-party tested. The certificate of analysis is published on the product page. I read it before I ordered.

That is the whole formula. One molecule. One clinical dose. Correctly delivered.

Before I ordered, I did one more thing. I called my retina specialist's office and I spoke to his nurse. I told her exactly what I was planning to add and I asked whether it would interact with the Vabysmo or with anything else in my protocol. She checked with my retina specialist and called me back the next day. His answer was that natural astaxanthin at twelve milligrams per day would not interact with anti-VEGF and I should feel free to add it if I wanted to. He asked her to make a note in my chart that I was doing so.

I ordered a bottle that afternoon. I took my first softgel with breakfast the next morning.

I want to tell you what changed and I want to be honest about it, because you deserve the honest version.

My injection schedule did not change. I still get Vabysmo every six weeks. That has not moved and I have not tried to make it move. When your retina specialist recommends an injection schedule for wet AMD, that is a medical decision made on the basis of your specific disease activity and it is not the kind of thing you renegotiate on the basis of how you feel.

What has changed is what I can see between the injections.

My spreadsheet has kept its receipts. Since I started CoraLume in June 2023, my visual acuity in the left eye — which had been declining for two years despite the injections controlling the wet component — has held. It has not gotten better. But for eighteen months it has not gotten worse either. That is the first eighteen-month stretch in three years where I have not lost a line on the eye chart.

The eye fatigue I used to feel at the end of a long day of reading or watching television has quieted. Not disappeared. Quieted. I can read a novel now for two hours without needing to stop and rest my eyes. Six months ago I could read for forty-five minutes.

The glare I used to get from oncoming headlights when I drove at night is softer at the edges. I still avoid highway driving after dark, and I probably always will. But driving to my daughter's house on a suburban road at seven in the evening no longer feels like something I have to steel myself for.

My retina specialist noticed at my most recent appointment. He looked at my OCT scan and my visual acuity and he asked me whether anything had changed in my routine. I told him about the CoraLume. He wrote it in the chart. He did not endorse it. He did not disendorse it. He said, whatever you have added, keep taking it.

I want to be very clear about what I am and am not telling you.

I am not telling you that CoraLume will let you reduce your injection frequency. I did not reduce mine and I have no intention of trying. My retina specialist controls my injection schedule based on my disease activity and that is not the piece of my protocol I am willing to experiment with.

I am not telling you that CoraLume will reverse existing central vision loss. It has not reversed mine.

I am not telling you that CoraLume replaces anti-VEGF. It does not. Nothing does.

I am telling you that the injections address one specific problem, and that if you are like I was in April 2023 — three hundred and eighteen appointments in, watching your visual acuity drop between injections that are perfectly controlling your wet component, asking your retina specialist what else you can do and being told to eat more spinach — there is a body of research your specialist has not brought up because it does not run through his exam room.

You have the same access to that research that I did.

You have the same option to add a maintenance layer to your protocol that I did.

CoraLume comes with a 90-day money-back guarantee. If your eye fatigue does not lift, if your night driving does not improve, if your visual acuity trend line between injections does not stabilize the way mine did — you send back a partially-used bottle and you do not pay. That is CoraLume's commitment.

Mine is this. Give it twelve full weeks alongside your injections. That is the amount of time astaxanthin needs to accumulate in retinal tissue at the concentrations the clinical trials measured. Any shorter and you are testing an incomplete dose. Keep your injection schedule exactly as your retina specialist has prescribed it. This is not that piece of your protocol.

One softgel with breakfast. That is the entire addition.

I am not writing this because anyone paid me to write it.

I am writing it because I spent thirty-two years running the books at a small firm, and when I retired I thought I was done vetting contracts. Then I got wet AMD, and I found out I was not done. I was going to spend the rest of my life vetting my own care, because nobody else was going to vet it for me.

Three hundred and eighteen appointments taught me that my retina specialist is a good doctor doing exactly what he was trained to do. My spreadsheet taught me that what he was trained to do is not the same as what my retina needs.

There is a second layer. It has been documented for two decades. Nobody in the pharmaceutical pipeline that trained my specialist has any financial reason to bring it up in the exam room.

I brought it up. I added it. I have been on it for eighteen months alongside my injections.

You have the same window.

He said we had discussed AREDS2 at my initial diagnosis and I had declined because the zinc bothered my stomach. He said beyond AREDS2, there was nothing else with the same level of evidence. He said to eat more spinach and to come back in six weeks.

I paid my copay. I walked out to my car. I drove home.

I sat at my kitchen table and I did what I have done every time in my life when a person in a position of authority has given me an answer that did not match what I was seeing in front of me.

I did the research.

Not on Facebook. Not on the AMD support groups where everyone tells you what worked for their sister-in-law. On PubMed. On the actual medical literature. The way I used to research zoning ordinances when the architects needed to know what they could build on a specific lot.

I spent six weeks reading.

Here is what I found.

The pivotal anti-VEGF trials — MARINA and ANCHOR, both published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2006 — established the current injection protocol for wet AMD. Those trials were carefully designed. The drug was Lucentis at the time. The protocol was monthly injections. The primary endpoint was preventing vision loss.

The trials succeeded. They showed that anti-VEGF injections significantly reduced the rate of vision loss in wet AMD patients compared to placebo. That is why we have the injection protocol we have now. That is why my Vabysmo appointment happens every six weeks. That is why my central macular thickness is stable.

But if you read the MARINA and ANCHOR papers themselves — not the marketing materials, the actual papers — you will find something the trial authors are explicit about.

The trials were designed to test one specific mechanism. Blocking vascular endothelial growth factor. Preventing the abnormal blood vessels from leaking and bleeding into the retina.

They were not designed to test protection of the photoreceptor cells.

They were not designed to test mitochondrial support.

They were not designed to test antioxidant delivery to the retinal tissue.

The MARINA authors themselves noted, in their discussion section, that a substantial subset of patients in the trial continued to lose visual acuity over the study period even when the neovascular component was well-controlled by the injections.

I recognized myself in that sentence.

Wet AMD has two things happening at the same time.

The first is the abnormal blood vessel growth and the leaking. That is what the injections address. That is why my central macular thickness is stable and my leak is controlled.

The second is the underlying oxidative damage to the photoreceptor cells themselves. That damage has been happening in my retina since before the wet component appeared. It is happening now, between injections. It has been happening in my mother's dry AMD for eight years and she has never had a wet event at all.

The injections were never designed to address the second thing.

Nothing my retina specialist has prescribed me has been addressing the second thing.

Nobody in my three hundred and eighteen appointments ever brought up the second thing until I brought it up myself.

Here is why.

The follow-up research on the underlying oxidative damage in AMD has been accumulating in the medical literature since the late 1990s. Peer-reviewed papers from research groups in the United States, Japan, and Northern Europe have documented that a specific class of antioxidants — carotenoids that cross the blood-retinal barrier and enter the photoreceptor cells themselves — can reach the tissue where the second problem is happening.

The most-studied molecule in that literature is astaxanthin.

Not lutein. Not zeaxanthin. Not the AREDS2 formula.

Astaxanthin.

The clinical trials on astaxanthin and retinal function have been running for more than two decades. They use a specific dose in a specific delivery format. Twelve milligrams per day, delivered in a fat carrier so the molecule can cross into the tissue where the oxidative damage is happening.

That research has never been incorporated into any pharmaceutical protocol for wet or dry AMD.

For a specific reason.

The pharmaceutical companies that make anti-VEGF drugs — Genentech, Regeneron, Roche — have every financial incentive in the world to fund research on molecules they can patent. Ranibizumab was patented. Aflibercept was patented. Faricimab, the drug in my Vabysmo, was patented. Each one generated billions of dollars in revenue.

Astaxanthin is a natural carotenoid produced by a microalgae called Haematococcus pluvialis. It cannot be patented by anyone. There is no company on the planet with a financial reason to spend forty million dollars proving that this molecule addresses the second problem in AMD.

So the research on the injection protocol got funded, and the research on the oxidative photoreceptor damage sat in the medical journals. Both bodies of research are real. Both are peer-reviewed. Only one of them ended up in the exam room where my retina specialist practices.

This is not a conspiracy. Nobody buried anything. The astaxanthin literature is right there in PubMed. Any retina specialist with a library card can read it.

But medicine does not run on library cards. Medicine runs on continuing-education seminars sponsored by pharmaceutical companies, drug-rep visits, and clinical guidelines issued by professional societies whose recommendations are shaped by what the pharmaceutical pipeline has funded. Nobody sends a drug rep to talk to a retina specialist about a natural algae extract. There is no professional society bulletin recommending a supplement that no member can bill through insurance. The pipeline that would carry astaxanthin from the medical literature into my monthly injection appointment simply does not exist, because there is no money moving through it.

That is the finding that made me stop reading and start ordering.

Before I tell you what I ordered, I want to say something plainly.

Nothing I have found in six weeks of reading changes anything about my injection schedule.

I still get Vabysmo every six weeks. I have not missed an appointment since I started. I do not plan to miss one. The injections are addressing the first problem — the vascular one — and that problem does not go away, and it does not stop being urgent, and the day I let it go untreated is the day my wet AMD comes back and takes what is left of my central vision in the left eye.

Astaxanthin does not address vascular leakage. It does not replace anti-VEGF. It is not an alternative to the injections. Nothing in the peer-reviewed literature suggests it does what the injections do.

What astaxanthin does is address the second problem — the oxidative photoreceptor damage — that the injections were never designed to touch.

The injections are the emergency response.

Astaxanthin is the maintenance layer that has been missing from my protocol for three years.

That is why I am taking both.

I want to be careful here, because I have spent enough time reading marketing materials to know that when a supplement claim sounds too good, it usually is.

The reason most astaxanthin products on the market do not produce the results in the clinical literature is that most of them are not the astaxanthin the clinical literature tested.

Three problems, in three bottles out of four on the shelf.

The first is source. Astaxanthin can be manufactured synthetically in a laboratory from petrochemical precursors. It looks similar to the natural molecule. It does not perform the same way in the human body. Synthetic astaxanthin is cheaper and is what fills most private-label bottles. The clinical trials did not use it.

The second is dose. The trials that produced measurable outcomes used twelve milligrams per day. Most retail bottles contain four milligrams. Some contain six. A four-milligram bottle is not a smaller dose of the trial protocol — it is a different intervention entirely.

The third is delivery. Astaxanthin is a fat-soluble molecule. For it to cross into the tissue where the damage is happening, it has to be delivered in a fat carrier. Most retail products are sold as dry powder in a hard capsule. The powder passes through the digestive tract without ever reaching the cells that need it.

If you have tried astaxanthin before and felt nothing, one of those three things was almost certainly the reason.

I spent a week researching brands. I read certificates of analysis. I compared source documentation. I looked at extraction methods, concentration, delivery format, and third-party testing. I applied the same methodology I used at the architectural firm when I was vetting subcontractors.

I chose CoraLume.

Twelve milligrams per softgel — the dose the human clinical trials actually used.

Natural astaxanthin from Haematococcus pluvialis microalgae, ocean-cultivated, not synthesized in a lab. The same source used in the peer-reviewed literature.

Suspended in a fat carrier so the molecule reaches the retinal tissue. Softgel, not dry capsule.

Every batch third-party tested. The certificate of analysis is published on the product page. I read it before I ordered.

That is the whole formula. One molecule. One clinical dose. Correctly delivered.

Before I ordered, I did one more thing. I called my retina specialist's office and I spoke to his nurse. I told her exactly what I was planning to add and I asked whether it would interact with the Vabysmo or with anything else in my protocol. She checked with my retina specialist and called me back the next day. His answer was that natural astaxanthin at twelve milligrams per day would not interact with anti-VEGF and I should feel free to add it if I wanted to. He asked her to make a note in my chart that I was doing so.

I ordered a bottle that afternoon. I took my first softgel with breakfast the next morning.

I want to tell you what changed and I want to be honest about it, because you deserve the honest version.

My injection schedule did not change. I still get Vabysmo every six weeks. That has not moved and I have not tried to make it move. When your retina specialist recommends an injection schedule for wet AMD, that is a medical decision made on the basis of your specific disease activity and it is not the kind of thing you renegotiate on the basis of how you feel.

What has changed is what I can see between the injections.

My spreadsheet has kept its receipts. Since I started CoraLume in June 2023, my visual acuity in the left eye — which had been declining for two years despite the injections controlling the wet component — has held. It has not gotten better. But for eighteen months it has not gotten worse either. That is the first eighteen-month stretch in three years where I have not lost a line on the eye chart.

The eye fatigue I used to feel at the end of a long day of reading or watching television has quieted. Not disappeared. Quieted. I can read a novel now for two hours without needing to stop and rest my eyes. Six months ago I could read for forty-five minutes.

The glare I used to get from oncoming headlights when I drove at night is softer at the edges. I still avoid highway driving after dark, and I probably always will. But driving to my daughter's house on a suburban road at seven in the evening no longer feels like something I have to steel myself for.

My retina specialist noticed at my most recent appointment. He looked at my OCT scan and my visual acuity and he asked me whether anything had changed in my routine. I told him about the CoraLume. He wrote it in the chart. He did not endorse it. He did not disendorse it. He said, whatever you have added, keep taking it.

I want to be very clear about what I am and am not telling you.

I am not telling you that CoraLume will let you reduce your injection frequency. I did not reduce mine and I have no intention of trying. My retina specialist controls my injection schedule based on my disease activity and that is not the piece of my protocol I am willing to experiment with.

I am not telling you that CoraLume will reverse existing central vision loss. It has not reversed mine.

I am not telling you that CoraLume replaces anti-VEGF. It does not. Nothing does.

I am telling you that the injections address one specific problem, and that if you are like I was in April 2023 — three hundred and eighteen appointments in, watching your visual acuity drop between injections that are perfectly controlling your wet component, asking your retina specialist what else you can do and being told to eat more spinach — there is a body of research your specialist has not brought up because it does not run through his exam room.

You have the same access to that research that I did.

You have the same option to add a maintenance layer to your protocol that I did.

CoraLume comes with a 90-day money-back guarantee. If your eye fatigue does not lift, if your night driving does not improve, if your visual acuity trend line between injections does not stabilize the way mine did — you send back a partially-used bottle and you do not pay. That is CoraLume's commitment.

Mine is this. Give it twelve full weeks alongside your injections. That is the amount of time astaxanthin needs to accumulate in retinal tissue at the concentrations the clinical trials measured. Any shorter and you are testing an incomplete dose. Keep your injection schedule exactly as your retina specialist has prescribed it. This is not that piece of your protocol.

One softgel with breakfast. That is the entire addition.

I am not writing this because anyone paid me to write it.

I am writing it because I spent thirty-two years running the books at a small firm, and when I retired I thought I was done vetting contracts. Then I got wet AMD, and I found out I was not done. I was going to spend the rest of my life vetting my own care, because nobody else was going to vet it for me.

Three hundred and eighteen appointments taught me that my retina specialist is a good doctor doing exactly what he was trained to do. My spreadsheet taught me that what he was trained to do is not the same as what my retina needs.

There is a second layer. It has been documented for two decades. Nobody in the pharmaceutical pipeline that trained my specialist has any financial reason to bring it up in the exam room.

I brought it up. I added it. I have been on it for eighteen months alongside my injections.

You have the same window.
